title: Dry Needling, Demystified
author: Natalie McAveney, PT, DPT
excerpt: It's one of the most-asked-about services I offer. Here's what it is, what it isn't, and who it helps.
body:
Trigger point dry needling is one of the most misunderstood tools in my toolbox — and one of the most effective for the right presentation.

A thin filiform needle is inserted into a taut band of muscle to elicit a local twitch response, which can reduce pain and restore normal muscle length. It is not acupuncture, though the needles look similar.

It tends to help most with stubborn trigger points that haven't responded to stretching or manual therapy alone — often in the neck, shoulders, hips, and calves.

title: What Actually Happens at Your First Visit
author: Natalie McAveney, PT, DPT
excerpt: No gowns, no waiting room, no 15-minute rush. Here's what a real first session looks like.
body:
A lot of people come to their first appointment expecting the pace of a typical clinic visit — quick intake, a few questions, handed off to an aide. That's not how this works.

Your first visit is 100% one-on-one, in a quiet private space, and it starts with actually listening. We'll go through your history, what you've already tried, and what your goals are — not just for pain relief, but for what you want to get back to doing.

From there we move: a real movement assessment, hands-on treatment where it's useful, and a plan you leave with, not just a folder of handouts.

title: Why Hypermobile Bodies Need a Different Approach to Pain
author: Natalie McAveney, PT, DPT
excerpt: Standard strengthening advice often falls short for hypermobile and EDS bodies. Here's what tends to actually help.
body:
If you've been told to just "strengthen it" and the pain keeps coming back, you're not alone — and you're not doing it wrong. Hypermobile joints move through a larger range than a typical strengthening program accounts for, which means stability has to be built differently.

For many of my patients with hypermobility spectrum disorder or EDS, the missing piece isn't more exercise — it's _where_ in the range that exercise happens, how breath and bracing are cued, and how much the nervous system trusts the joint to begin with.

A few things I look at in almost every hypermobile evaluation:

- Where in the joint's range does control break down first?
- Is breath being used to create stability, or is it being held?
- Are we training the end-range, not just avoiding it?

None of this replaces a full evaluation, but if this sounds familiar, it might be worth a conversation.
